content: The optimal treatment strategy for adult T-cell leukemia (ATL) is determined by the specific clinical variant of the disease. For patients with chronic or smoldering ATL, management typically involves observation, skin-directed therapies, or a combination of zidovudine and interferon therapy. Acute ATL patients are generally treated with chemotherapy, supportive care, allogeneic stem cell transplantation, or a combination of zidovudine and interferon therapy. Patients with adult T-cell lymphoma are usually managed with chemotherapy, supportive care, or allogeneic stem cell transplantation. Management of Chronic/Smoldering Adult T-Cell Leukemia Patients with chronic or smoldering ATL may be managed through observation and close follow-up to monitor for any symptomatic deterioration. Follow-up evaluations for these patients may include: A complete history and physical examination. Measurement of serum calcium levels. Blood urea nitrogen (BUN) levels. Serum creatinine levels. Serum lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) levels. Chest and abdominal CT scans. For localized cutaneous lesions, skin-directed therapies may include: Topical corticosteroids. Topical chemotherapy, such as mechlorethamine. Local radiation therapy (8–36 Gy). Topical retinoids, including bexarotene or tazarotene. Phototherapy (UVB or narrowband UVB for patch/thin plaques; PUVA for thicker plaques). Topical imiquimod. For patients undergoing zidovudine and interferon combination therapy: Response to therapy should be evaluated after two months of treatment initiation. Patients who respond to therapy should continue zidovudine and interferon therapy. Patients who do not respond to therapy should be managed with either chemotherapy or supportive care, depending on patient preference. Criteria for complete remission in ATL patients include: Absence of lymphadenopathy. Absence of hepatomegaly and splenomegaly. Absence of cutaneous lesions. Absence of malignant cells on peripheral blood smear. Absence of malignant cells on bone marrow biopsy. Management of Acute Adult T-Cell Leukemia First-line chemotherapeutic regimens for acute ATL include: Cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, and prednisone (CHOP). Cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, etoposide, and prednisone (CHOEP). Dose-adjusted EPOCH (etoposide, prednisone, vincristine, cyclophosphamide, and doxorubicin). HyperCVAD (cyclophosphamide, vincristine, doxorubicin, and dexamethasone) alternating with high-dose methotrexate and cytarabine. Patients who respond to first-line chemotherapy should be considered for allogeneic stem cell transplantation. For patients who do not respond to initial chemotherapy, second-line chemotherapeutic agents may be used, including: Bendamustine. Belinostat. Brentuximab vedotin (for systemic CD30+ peripheral T-cell lymphoma). DHAP (dexamethasone, cisplatin, cytarabine). ESHAP (etoposide, methylprednisolone, cytarabine, cisplatin). Dose-adjusted EPOCH. GDP (gemcitabine, dexamethasone, cisplatin). GemOx (gemcitabine, oxaliplatin). ICE (ifosfamide, carboplatin, etoposide). Pralatrexate. Romidepsin. Patients who respond to second-line chemotherapy should also be considered for allogeneic stem cell transplantation. Management of Adult T-Cell Lymphoma First-line chemotherapeutic regimens for adult T-cell lymphoma are similar to those for acute ATL and include: CHOP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, prednisone). CHOEP (cyclophosphamide, doxorubicin, vincristine, etoposide, prednisone). Dose-adjusted EPOCH. HyperCVAD alternating with high-dose methotrexate and cytarabine. Patients who respond to first-line chemotherapy should be considered for allogeneic stem cell transplantation. For those who do not respond, second-line chemotherapeutic agents, as listed above, may be used. Supportive Therapy Prophylaxis Against Opportunistic Infections Sulfamethoxazole/trimethoprim prophylaxis is recommended for adult T-cell leukemia patients to prevent opportunistic infections.
